item.dc:creator: Hao Mo, Liying Yang, Shumin Yao, Xinxing Yu, Ajian Liu, Xudong Mao, Yanyan Liang

item.title: AdaptLSTM: Efficient Adaptive Online Learning for Cloud Workload Forecasting under Distribution Drift
item.description: arXiv:2610.12265v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate workload forecasting is critical for elastic resource provisioning in web-scale cloud services, where distribution shifts driven by viral content, product launches, and user behavior degrade offline-trained models rapidly. Naive online learning recovers accuracy but incurs prohibitive per-step compute cost. We propose AdaptLSTM, an adaptive online framework that detects drift via validation-calibrated thresholds and applies selective, targeted updates. On the Alibaba Machine Trace, AdaptLSTM recovers 54\% of Naive Online's improvement at 20\% cost ($2.7\times$ efficiency, $p=0.002$ over 10 seeds). On the more volatile Container Trace, it achieves 96\% at 20\% cost ($4.8\times$ efficiency, $+75\%$ MAE reduction over Static). Unlike classical drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM, Page-Hinkley) which fail to trigger on regression-scale error streams, AdaptLSTM fires 42 times over 301 steps and outperforms matched-budget baselines. Wall-clock profiling shows $1.33\times$ throughput gain and 45\% update-time reduction. The framework is model-agnostic: identical Pareto patterns hold for LSTM, GRU, and Transformer backbones.
item.dc:creator: Xinhua Miao, Bowei Yang, Zhengong Cai

item.title: SelectArena: A Modern Benchmark for Feature Selection on Real-world Tabular Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.13644v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Selecting a subset of features (columns) from a tabular dataset is a ubiquitous challenge in real-world applications. Industry experts seek to minimize model training costs, climate scientists require an interpretable subset of factors to understand extreme weather events, and clinicians need to choose among diagnostic tests due to financial and time constraints. When looking at the scientific literature to determine which feature selection method to use, practitioners across domains face an unrepresentative landscape of benchmarking. Despite extensive research, existing feature selection benchmarks provide limited guidance because they rely on outdated models, ad hoc evaluation protocols, or artificially generated data that do not reflect real-world problems. To close the gap between scientific benchmarking and real-world applications, we introduce SelectArena, a modern benchmark for feature selection. We compare 15 widely used feature selection methods on 71 manually curated real-world tabular datasets, covering classification and regression problems, using standardized evaluation protocols and state-of-the-art tabular (foundation) models. Our results reveal clear trade-offs across predictive performance, runtime, stability, and validity. Tree-based methods, CART and RFImportance, along with F-Test are Pareto-optimal when taking into account predictive performance and runtime. F-Test, information-theory-, and distance-based methods lead on stability and validity, with F-Test emerging as a balanced choice across our metrics. Search-based methods are slow, unstable and achieve low performance. SelectArena turns these findings into practical guidance and, as an extensible platform, supports future feature selection research.
item.dc:creator: Bastian Sch\"afer, Dominika Matus, Lennart Purucker, Ricardo Knauer, Erik Rodner, Frank Hutter, Anton Sokolov, Arnaud Liefooghe

item.title: Guarded Block Transfers for Polytope Distance: Linear Convergence with Explicit Constants and Gap-Certified Screening for SVM Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.15829v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hard-margin SVM training is the distance problem between two convex hulls, which the Triangle Algorithm (TA) solves with a certified duality gap. We propose \emph{guarded block transfers}: $k$ Mitchell--Demyanov--Malozemov (MDM) transfers per scan are aggregated into one exact line search, guarded by a comparison with the single best transfer at a cost independent of the number of points $n$, and replaced by an away step when the leading transfer is capacity-clipped. On the Minkowski-difference polytope, where the objective is $1$-strongly convex, we prove global linear convergence with explicit constants and no combinatorial swap-step bounds; the per-step contraction is $k$-independent and only the drop-count bound grows with $k$, so aggregation is provably safe while the saving in scans is measured, not proved. Since the TA certificate is the Frank--Wolfe gap divided by the current distance, gap-safe screening applies, and we bound the iteration after which it has removed every zero-weight point off the optimal faces by $O\!\left(\tfrac{k}{\rho}\log\tfrac{1}{\tau}\right)$ up to logarithmic factors in the geometry, $\rho$ the rate constant and $\tau$ the optimal-face margin. On five LIBSVM benchmarks, with fairer baselines than our submission, the solver matches the baselines to four or five digits wherever both converge, ties LIBSVM on sparse-support hard margins and beats our blended pairwise conditional gradients (BPCG). But our full-cache sequential minimal optimisation (SMO) code ties or beats it on kernel $L_2$ margins, LIBLINEAR's dual solver is up to $4.5\times$ faster on the separable $L_2$ margin, and our solver is one to three orders of magnitude slower than LIBLINEAR's Newton solver on dense-support $L_2$ margins and than LIBSVM on a nearly touching kernel hull. Its edge is the certificate, not speed.
item.dc:creator: Mayank Gupta

item.title: Error Correction in Trained TTT Layers
item.description: arXiv:2610.16268v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.
item.dc:creator: Yuhe Hu

item.title: LoongSage: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
item.description: arXiv:2610.16352v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.
item.dc:creator: LoongSage Team, Bowei Song, Caiwei Zhao, Chuwen Liu, Dechuang Gu, Dong Fang, Feiyu Xie, Huaiyu Li, Hui Zhang, Jian Tian, Jian Wang, Jie Zhao, Liguang Li, Maoyun Wang, Meiyan Yang, Minghan Zhu, Pai Liu, Pandeng Yao, Renbao Tian, Ru Yang, Shuai Jia, Shuai Tan, Shuailong Li, Shuliang Li, Teng Jin, Tianze Yang, Wenbo Cui, Wenjing Bai, Wenkang Wu, Xiaowei Jiang, Xiaoyi Dong, Yanpeng Wang, Yanwen Wang, Yaohui Ma, Yawen Wang, Yihang Zhang, Yingjie Yan, Zhanbiao Lian, Zhenyu Lu, Zhida Hu, Zhihui Hao, Zhihui Hu, Zhiwen Xiao, Zhiyi Gao, Zhongwei Qi, Zhuangzhuang Wu, Ziqian Liu, Ziyue Zheng

item.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
item.description: arXiv:2610.17697v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.
item.dc:creator: Rodney Lafuente-Mercado, Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, James Shiffer, Saadia Gabriel, Pavel Izmailov

item.title: Follow the Perturbed Leader for Linear Bandits: $\sqrt{T}$ Regret over General Action Sets
item.description: arXiv:2610.17818v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give the first adversarial linear bandit algorithm based on Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) that achieves $\sqrt{T}$ regret over general action sets. Our algorithm attains $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d^{5/4}\sqrt{T})$ regret using only linear optimization oracles, and the near-optimal $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d\sqrt{T})$ regret when an optimal-design exploration distribution is further available. This improves on the $T^{2/3}$ regret of the FTPL algorithm of Dani and Hayes (2006) for general action sets, and generalizes the $\sqrt{T}$ regret of L\'evy et al. (2026) over two special action sets (hypercube and Euclidean ball). Compared to previous oracle-efficient linear bandit algorithms based on continuous exponential weights, the FTPL approach generally has better computational efficiency, and is much simpler to implement. The key algorithmic element is a perturbation distribution that adapts to the past reward estimators. Its simplest form, an adaptive Gaussian perturbation, is straightforward to implement and already attains the regret bound above. We further extend it to two general constructions, random-weighting and elliptical perturbations, each covering distributions from light tails (Gaussian) to heavy tails (Student-$t_2$). On the technical side, we develop a systematic way to analyze the stability term in the FTPL regret through the Fisher information of the perturbation distribution. This builds a general framework for FTPL beyond existing ones such as the hazard rate and the FTRL-FTPL duality.
item.dc:creator: Chen-Yu Wei

item.title: Agentic-MatriBO: Capability-Compiled Agentic Bayesian Optimization for Materials and Chemical Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.17832v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Materials and chemical optimization must choose the next synthesis, characterization, or high-fidelity simulation from sequential observations under a limited budget. Large language models can use task knowledge to propose adjustments, but composing surrogates, acquisition functions, and search strategies is constrained by compatibility, parameter dependencies, and evidence requirements. We present Agentic-MatriBO, a capability-compiled agentic Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that represents BO components and selection conditions as composable capabilities. A language policy proposes BO recipes and candidate plans; a compiler checks proposals against the registered capability catalog; and a deterministic execution layer validates and commits candidates. Oracle observations are stored in research memory and inform later rounds. We compare Agentic-MatriBO with eight baselines on four offline finite candidate pools---COF, PCE10, Buchwald--Hartwig (BH), and Suzuki--Miyaura---using five seeds per condition; results are reported descriptively. Across the four tasks, Agentic-MatriBO has the best mean endpoint quality after orienting each objective so that higher is better. On COF, it reaches the tabulated optimum in all five seeds both in the end-to-end comparison and after shared initialization, where it also retains an advantage in cumulative quality. Its normalized area under the best-so-far quality curve during the BO stage (nAUC-BO) is substantially higher on COF, near parity with the best baseline on PCE10 and BH, and lower on Suzuki. COF ablations show that removing the capability compiler or evidence gate coincides with lower cumulative quality and fewer exact-optimum hits. The framework provides an inspectable interface for evidence-conditioned BO adaptation.
item.dc:creator: Yu Zeng, Yuchuan Chen, Ziyue Zhang, Zijian Wei, Yanyi Su, Guojiang Zhao, Hongshuai Wang, Zhifeng Gao

item.title: Kwai Summary Attention V2 Technical Report
item.description: arXiv:2610.18654v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Summary-token architectures such as Kwai Summary Attention (KSA) compress distant context into learnable Summary token per chunk, and hybrid variants interleave these layers with full attention to retain exact access to the original text. In such hybrid KSA-Full architecture, the interleaving inserted summary tokens are served as a streaming flow role across different layers. Although effective, however, it also introduce some bottlenecks: (1) the different layers summary compression chunk must be same, therefore hard to reach a flexible KV Cache compression, e.g., different layer set different summary compression chunk window. (2) in the full-attention layers, the summary token introduced additional computation cost, but such layer ignore them and still pay quadratic prefilling, therefore unfriendly to the computation side. Motivated by them, we developed the KSA V2, which not only achieves a more flexible KV cache memory compression but also reduces the computation cost in Full attention layer. Specifically, we found that the summary tokens can serve two roles: the KV memory and sparse indexer.
item.dc:creator: OneRec Team, Chenglong Chu, Guohong Mu, Guowang Zhang, Hao Peng, Hui Wang, Jian Liang, Jiangxia Cao, Jiao Ou, Jiaxin Deng, Lu Ren, Muhao Wei, Ruiming Tang, Tianle Xu, Wenwu Ou, Xingmei Wang, Zhixin Ling, Zhiyuan Liang, Ziqi Wang, Chaoyi Ma, Haixiao Gao, Kuo Cai, Renpu Liu, Ruochen Yang, Wenlong Xu, Xinqi Jin, Yan Sun, Yifan Wang, Yingzhi He, Yiyu Wang, Yusen Huo, Zhaojie Liu, Zihan Zhou

item.title: SP$^2$ec: Adaptive Self-Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.18735v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative Decoding (SD) has demonstrated its efficacy in accelerating large language model inference, but for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), the diverse input modalities make it difficult for a small trained drafter to achieve consistently high throughput. Self-speculative decoding reuses parts of the target model as a drafter which retains the multi-modal capability of the VLMs, yet its efficiency depends on choosing a suitable draft configuration for each prompt. We propose Single-Peak SPeculative decoding (SP$^2$ec), a training-free bandit algorithm that adapts the draft configuration during generation. SP$^2$ec exploits the single-peak throughput pattern observed in existing self-speculative methods, including SWIFT, KnapSpec, SpecVLM, and our simple cosSim. Our algorithmic design explicitly minimizes a novel notion of wall-time regret for each given query, corresponding to the empirical wall-time latency. Theoretical guarantees on the wall-time regret show that SP$^2$ec can exploit the optimal draft configuration, with negligible exploration cost. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B across visual and textual tasks show consistent improvements of up to 11\% over the original self-speculative methods, demonstrating the wide applicability of the proposed SP$^2$ec algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Yuqi Huang, Xingyao Li, Yunlong Hou, Fengzhuo Zhang, Jiachun Pan, Vincent Y. F. Tan

item.title: Statistical Vignettes on the Grokking Phenomenon
item.description: arXiv:2610.18811v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we study grokking in a simple, analytically tractable setting whose rich phenomenology allows us to disentangle the effects of initialization, signal strength, weight decay, sample size, and input dimension. These factors can produce superficially similar learning curves through distinct mechanisms, complicating their interpretation. Our analysis distinguishes early fitting through nuisance features, core feature learning, and delayed generalization. We identify sharp conditions under which grokking provably occurs and derive analytic asymptotic expressions for the lengths of the generalization plateaus. Our results also characterize regimes of early generalization and failure to reach a prescribed test accuracy target. We show that the interpolation edge constitutes a distinct dynamical regime, where vanishing spectral gaps separate core learning from generalization, helping clarify the role of proximity to interpolation in existing accounts of grokking. The resulting picture is analogous to fast and slow phases in chemical kinetics and suggests that the lazy-to-rich transition discussed in the literature may reflect a similar separation of dynamical time scales. Our theoretical results are faithfully supported by extensive experiments.
item.dc:creator: Baye Malick Gning, Elvis Dohmatob

item.title: Riding the Fixed-Point Curve: Image Classification in the Continuous Thought Machine
item.description: arXiv:2610.19220v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) is a recurrent network that attends to inputs and makes predictions based on the synchronization between its neurons. On tasks spanning many domains, it displays emergent thought processes that have not been explained. We report a number of findings about how the CTM classifies images, focusing on ImageNet. Thinking steps are attracting but strongly non-normal maps exhibiting balanced amplification (Murphy and Miller, 2009); while attraction is already present at CTM initialization, training highly promotes non-normality. By Banach's theorem, the neural state thus has a locally unique attracting fixed point, which moves at every step, and the thought trajectory is the curve these fixed points trace, followed one tick behind. Most of that curve's motion is shared across images, and visible as a previously reported traveling wave of activity across neurons. The attention schedule along the thought is largely generic: shuffling queries across images at every tick costs only 7 percent of classification accuracy, while image-independent increments predict the next query with R^2 = 0.98 (held out). Our results suggest that the CTM has found a single strategy to process all ImageNet images.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Hannagan

item.title: Fully sequential Gaussian process regression for preference learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.19391v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study continuous global optimization problems in which the objective function cannot be directly evaluated; rather, we observe only which of two selected design points appears to perform better, subject to noise. Such comparisons complicate the use of Gaussian process regression because they yield non-Gaussian posteriors. We consider a fully sequential approximation, based on moment-matching, that yields a fast closed-form update of the metamodel's mean and covariance. We then propose DOVE, a fully sequential sampling policy that combines an information gain criterion with randomized sampling designed to control error accumulation. Under fairly standard regularity conditions, we prove convergence rates for both statistical error and expected simple regret that depend on kernel smoothness. To our knowledge, these are the first such rates for fully sequential approximate Bayesian inference in continuous global optimization.
item.dc:creator: Ilya O. Ryzhov

item.title: TANGO: RNA Topology and Geometry Co-Design
item.description: arXiv:2610.20277v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Designing RNA sequences that satisfy target tertiary-structure objectives is an important problem in RNA engineering, with broad applications in synthetic biology and therapeutics. Existing 3D RNA design methods have made substantial progress, but they largely treat the target fold as a geometry-only objective. This is incomplete for RNA, whose functional folds are specified not only by tertiary geometry but also by secondary base-pairing topology. We therefore formulate RNA inverse design as a topology-and-geometry co-design problem and propose TANGO, a multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for this task. TANGO adopts a staged curriculum: it first learns a topology-aware policy from secondary-structure targets, then transfers this policy to tertiary-structure targets to train a general co-design model, and finally applies frontier-guided fine-tuning to refine target-specific trade-offs among secondary-structure fidelity, tertiary-structure fidelity, and sequence diversity. Experiments show that TANGO generates diverse and novel designs, improving tertiary- and secondary-structure performance by 18.3% and 52.7%, respectively, over the strongest baseline.
item.dc:creator: Tianmeng Hu, Biao Luo, Ke Li

item.title: Learnable Hodge-Laplacian Driven Mixture of Experts for Steady-PDE Surrogates on Coarse Unstructured Meshes
item.description: arXiv:2610.20585v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Current approaches for steady partial differential equations surrogate models on unstructured meshes apply a single mixing mechanism to the whole solution. This paper proposes an architecture that partitions the solution among vanilla transformer experts, each focused on a different spectral scale. The partition is built from a discrete Hodge Laplacian $L_0=\star_0^{-1} d_0^{\top}\star_1 d_0$, that serves as a fitting layer measuring high-frequency content. A gating mechanism takes the mesh as input and produces the per-vertex weights that recombine the expert outputs. AirFRANS is a steady Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) airfoil benchmark. We evaluate our approach in a reduced remeshed version of the benchmark with each unstructured mesh counting 9.6K faces and 4.9K vertices. We compare our approach with the Transolver on the same dataset and dataset slit. Our approach reduces relative $L_2$ error by 31% and interior mean squared error by 47%.
item.dc:creator: Stavros Nousias, Akis Nousias, Konstantinos Gkrispanis

item.title: Spectral Indistinguishability and Learning-Curve Identifiability in Quadratic Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.20678v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Motivated by information-organization sculpting, we study spectral summaries and scalar learning curves in centered quadratic networks. We construct analytic positive input densities with Gaussian one- and two-coordinate marginals. Their complete fourth-moment operators are orthogonally intertwined by a map fixing the entire diagonal teacher algebra, giving equal anchored spectral measures. For selected common teachers with a nonzero cycle invariant, their factorized loss curves differ because the map does not preserve matrix multiplication. Cycle length $r$, which can be arbitrarily large, gives $O(\varepsilon^r)$ contrast uniformly in training time for each fixed construction. For a supplied pair, noisy scalar loss queries require order $\varepsilon^{-2r}$ observations, while bounded initialization interventions with scalar gradient readouts require order $\varepsilon^{-2}$. A shared-input score, equal to a paired-gradient difference, attains the optimal input-sample exponent without knowing the teacher. An explicit family of diverging auxiliary teacher scales instead admits a nonzero finite limiting contrast at coupling $1/\log L$. Conversely, for Gaussian inputs and a rationally independent teacher spectrum, one exact scalar loss curve identifies the initial predictor up to sign conjugation. Within this rationally independent class, with nonzero diagonal inverse-state error in every coordinate and calibrated time and loss scales, it also identifies the unknown teacher spectrum and active dimension, modulo simultaneous rotations. For fixed dimension and distinct unordered teacher sums, dimension-minimal exact observations give generic joint local recovery. Finite exact global bounds hold for a known teacher and, on the active class, under a blind dimension cap. Exact certificates and full-weight replay verify the construction; numerical inverse checks reveal severe ill-conditioning.
item.dc:creator: Dekun Yang

item.title: SALTO: Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators for Nonlinear Event Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.21049v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Learned dynamical models can accurately predict trajectories while producing unreliable sensitivities when differentiated or transposed, limiting their use in inverse problems and scientific decision-making. Classical adjoints provide exact local derivatives, but a single adjoint cannot represent the nonlinear response of a system to a family of finite-amplitude perturbations. We introduce SALTO (Solver-Anchored Lifted Transfer Operators), a Koopman-based framework for inferring finite-amplitude sources. In the lifted space, the nonlinear dynamics are approximated by a linear propagator, and its transpose carries each sensor backward in a single solve. The result is a reusable lifted adjoint that predicts the measurement produced by any candidate localized event with one encoder pass and an inner product. To give the model the simulator's exact local behavior, SALTO imposes three structural constraints: it anchors the physical-state dynamics to the simulator's linearized propagator, centers the learned observables so that they vanish to second order at the reference state, and uses a block-triangular lifted propagator. These constraints guarantee that the model reduces to the simulator's tangent dynamics and classical adjoint as the amplitude vanishes, while the learned observables carry only the finite-amplitude correction. On three nonlinear PDE systems, SALTO predicts the measurements of finite-amplitude sources to within 2-8% where the classical adjoint is in error by 41-165%, recovers source position and intensity from sparse sensors nearly as accurately as inversion through the solver, and samples the joint posterior of two interacting sources, matching the solver's posterior on reaction-diffusion at a twentieth of its cost. One trained model serves new sensor layouts and measurement times with a single backward solve.
item.dc:creator: Qi Wang, Rylie Foster

item.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
item.description: arXiv:2610.21337v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) effectively transfers capabilities from a teacher to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts. However, generating complete student rollouts and computing teacher feedback for every token make OPD computationally expensive. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.
item.dc:creator: Zhengxin Zhang, Maosen Tang, Ning Wang, Changhao Li, Jingren Zhou, Bo Dai, Sainyam Galhotra, Alex Townsend, Claire Cardie

item.title: Router Drift Control: Mitigating Off-Policy Degradation in Mixture-of-Experts Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.21682v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can become off-policy due to training-inference mismatch, mini-batch updates, and asynchronous training. The resulting mismatch is especially harmful in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, where rollout-training discrepancies can change routing decisions and lead to router drift. Rollout Routing Replay (R3) mitigates this mismatch by reusing expert selections from the rollout stage during training. Our analysis shows that routing replay introduces gradient bias by losing contributions from experts selected by the training router but not the rollout router. To address this, we propose Router Drift Control (RDC), which uses routing disagreement between rollout and training as a signal of off-policy staleness and selectively rejects high-drift responses. The sequence-level filtering avoids gradient bias introduced by replay while preserving native expert selection and the associated learning signals for retained responses. Experiments show that RDC achieves larger gains as policy staleness increases and remains effective in asynchronous RL. In asynchronous training, RDC combined with Truncated Importance Sampling (TIS) improves the average peak validation accuracy across AIME 2024 and AIME 2025 by 5.5 points over TIS and 4.5 points over R3.
item.dc:creator: Liangyao Jin, Zhixin Wang, Liming Liu, Mingjun Zhang, Zhengzhou Zhu, Fangcheng Fu, Jinlong Hou, Yuan Cheng, Xiaohe Hu, Ping Zhang, Siyuan Feng

item.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.21810v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
item.dc:creator: Donghoon Han, Minseop Jung, Dong Woo Kwak, SeungJae Lee, Junhoo Lee

item.title: Beyond Fixed Acquisition Functions: Temporal Difference Active Learning for Perturbation Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2610.22122v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Genetic and drug perturbation screens are important tools for elucidating disease mechanisms and validating therapeutic targets, but experimental costs limit the number of candidates that can be tested. Existing perturbation screening methods typically update the surrogate model with feedback while keeping the acquisition function fixed, limiting their ability to adapt selection to different response landscapes. Experimental feedback reveals current hits and informs subsequent selection by updating candidate predictions, providing a training signal for learning how to select experiments. We formulate budgeted perturbation discovery as a sequential decision problem and propose Temporal Difference Active Learning (TDAL), which learns an acquisition function online through temporal difference learning from a single screening trajectory, accounting for current hits and future discoveries. TDAL uses the Hellinger distance between hit probabilities for unmeasured candidates before and after an experiment to weight successor value, and reuses measured outcomes through leave-batch-out (LBO) to construct virtual transitions and alleviate training data scarcity. Across eight public screens spanning single, double, and triple perturbations under varied experimental configurations, TDAL achieves an average rank of 1.63 among eleven methods and ranks first on four tasks, demonstrating its adaptability across response landscapes.
item.dc:creator: Xudong Zhang, Jianzhe Li, Yitong Tang, Peijie Zhou

item.title: Accelerated Gradient Methods for Nonconvex Optimization: Escape Trajectories From Strict Saddle Points and Convergence to Local Minima
item.description: arXiv:2307.07030v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper considers the problem of understanding the behavior of a general class of accelerated gradient methods on smooth nonconvex functions. Motivated by some recent works that have proposed effective algorithms, based on Polyak's heavy ball method and the Nesterov accelerated gradient method, to achieve convergence to a local minimum of nonconvex functions, this work proposes a broad class of Nesterov-type accelerated methods and puts forth a rigorous study of these methods encompassing the escape from saddle points and convergence to local minima through both an asymptotic and a non-asymptotic analysis. In the asymptotic regime, this paper answers an open question of whether Nesterov's accelerated gradient method (NAG) with variable momentum parameter avoids strict saddle points almost surely. This work also develops two metrics of asymptotic rates of convergence and divergence, and evaluates these two metrics for several popular standard accelerated methods such as the NAG and Nesterov's accelerated gradient with constant momentum (NCM) near strict saddle points. In the non-asymptotic regime, this work provides an analysis that leads to the "linear" exit time estimates from strict saddle neighborhoods for trajectories of these accelerated methods as well the necessary conditions for the existence of such trajectories. Finally, this work studies a sub-class of accelerated methods that can converge in convex neighborhoods of nonconvex functions with a near optimal rate to a local minimum and at the same time this sub-class offers superior saddle-escape behavior compared to that of NAG.
item.dc:creator: Rishabh Dixit, Mert Gurbuzbalaban, Waheed U. Bajwa

item.title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning-Based UAV Pathfinding for Obstacle Avoidance in Stochastic Environment
item.description: arXiv:2310.16659v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Traditional methods plan feasible paths for multiple agents in the stochastic environment. However, the methods' iterations with the changes in the environment result in computation complexities, especially for the decentralized agents without a centralized planner. Although reinforcement learning provides a plausible solution because of the generalization for different environments, it struggles with enormous agent-environment interactions in training. Here, we propose a novel centralized training with decentralized execution method based on multi-agent reinforcement learning, which is improved based on the idea of model predictive control. In our approach, agents communicate only with the centralized planner to make decentralized decisions online in the stochastic environment. Furthermore, considering the communication constraint with the centralized planner, each agent plans feasible paths through the extended observation, which combines information on neighboring agents based on the distance-weighted mean field approach. Inspired by the rolling optimization approach of model predictive control, we conduct multi-step value convergence in multi-agent reinforcement learning to enhance the training efficiency, which reduces the expensive interactions in convergence. Experiment results in both comparison, ablation, and real-robot studies validate the effectiveness and generalization performance of our method.
item.dc:creator: Qizhen Wu, Kexin Liu, Lei Chen, Jinhu L\"u

item.title: Deep conditional distribution learning via conditional F\"ollmer flow
item.description: arXiv:2402.01460v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce an ordinary differential equation (ODE) based deep generative method for learning conditional distributions, named Conditional F\"ollmer Flow. Starting from a standard Gaussian distribution, the proposed flow could approximate the target conditional distribution very well when the time is close to 1. For effective implementation, we discretize the flow with Euler's method where we estimate the velocity field nonparametrically using a deep neural network. Furthermore, we also establish the convergence result for the Wasserstein-2 distance between the distribution of the learned samples and the target conditional distribution, providing the first comprehensive end-to-end error analysis for conditional distribution learning via ODE flow. Our numerical experiments showcase its effectiveness across a range of scenarios, from standard nonparametric conditional density estimation problems to more intricate challenges involving image data, illustrating its superiority over various existing conditional density estimation methods.
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Chang, Zhao Ding, Yuling Jiao, Ruoxuan Li, Jerry Zhijian Yang

item.title: Paint Outside the Box: Synthesizing and Selecting Training Data for Visual Grounding
item.description: arXiv:2412.00684v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Visual grounding aims to localize the image regions based on a textual query. Given the difficulty of large-scale data curation, we investigate how to effectively learn visual grounding under data-scarce settings in this paper. To address the data scarcity, we propose a novel framework, POBF (Paint Outside the Box and Filter). POBF synthesizes images by inpainting outside the box, tackling a label misalignment issue encountered in previous works. Furthermore, POBF leverages an innovative filtering scheme to select the most effective training data. This scheme combines a hardness score and an overfitting score, balanced by a penalty term. Extensive experiments across four benchmark datasets demonstrate that POBF consistently improves performance, achieving an average gain of 5.83\% over the real-data-only method and outperforming leading baselines by 2.29\%-3.85\% in accuracy. Additionally, we validate the robustness and generalizability of POBF across various generative models, training data sizes, and model architectures.
item.dc:creator: Zilin Du, Haoxin Li, Jianfei Yu, Boyang Li

item.title: Rethinking Negative Prompting for Concept Suppression: Unconditional Anchoring and Localized Guidance
item.description: arXiv:2412.07658v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Text-to-image diffusion models have rapidly transitioned from research prototypes to widely deployed tools. Along with their impressive capabilities, these models can also generate harmful or undesirable content (e.g., NSFW imagery), motivating practical mechanisms for removing such concepts. Negative prompting, which uses the negative-prompt prediction as the guidance anchor, is among the most widely used mechanisms for steering sampling trajectories away from unwanted concepts. However, for jailbreak prompts, it can fail in a regime we refer to as \emph{guidance collapse}, where the model's denoising predictions for the prompt and negative prompt become similar, so that the guidance difference driving negative prompting vanishes and the guided prediction degenerates to the negative-prompt prediction, undermining suppression. To fix this issue, we propose TraSCE (Trajectory Steering for ConcEpt Suppression), a training-free inference-time method that makes negative prompting reliable under guidance collapse. TraSCE combines two complementary components: (i) unconditional anchoring, which makes the fallback under guidance collapse a neutral unconditional prediction rather than the negative-prompt prediction, and (ii) an alignment-localized steering step, which deliberately induces this collapse for adversarial prompts and steers the sample to the unconditional fallback, while remaining minimally intrusive on benign prompts. We evaluate TraSCE on adversarial prompt benchmarks targeting nudity and violence, and further demonstrate its applicability to suppressing artistic styles and objects. Across these settings, TraSCE substantially improves the robustness of negative prompting to jailbreak prompts without any training, weight updates, or pre-collected concept-specific data (prompts or images), while keeping the impact on general image quality small.
item.dc:creator: Anubhav Jain, Takashi Shibuya, Yuya Kobayashi, Yuhta Takida, Nasir Memon, Julian Togelius, Yuki Mitsufuji

item.title: What is causal about causal models and representations?
item.description: arXiv:2501.19335v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Causal Bayesian networks are often described as causal because they support reasoning about interventions. Yet interventions are defined in the mathematical model, whereas the resulting model predictions concern the effects of actions in the real world. Consequently, whether and how a causal model makes falsifiable predictions about the effects of actions depends on how actions are interpreted as interventions. This requires specifying which actions correspond to which interventions, a step that is frequently left implicit. We develop a formal framework that separates a causal model from the data-generating process it aims to describe and formalizes interpretations connecting actions to interventions. Within this framework, we prove an impossibility result: no interpretation can simultaneously satisfy a collection of desirable properties while remaining non-circular. Under a circular interpretation, every model that fits the observational distribution is interventionally valid, so no experiment can falsify it. We analyze several non-circular alternatives and discuss implications for falsification, causal discovery, causal representation learning, and causal abstraction. More broadly, our framework provides a way to make assumptions about the connections between actions and interventions explicit and to reason formally about the empirical content of causal models.
item.dc:creator: Frederik Hytting J{\o}rgensen, Luigi Gresele, Sebastian Weichwald

item.title: Gabor-Enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Fast Simulations of Acoustic Wavefields
item.description: arXiv:2502.17134v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have gained attention for solving partial differential equations, including the scattered Helmholtz equation, due to their flexibility and mesh-free formulation. However, their performance suffers from low-frequency bias, particularly in high-frequency wavefield simulations, limiting convergence speed and accuracy. To address this, we propose a novel and simplified PINN framework that incorporates explicit, trainable Gabor basis functions to efficiently capture the localized and oscillatory nature of wavefields. Unlike previous Gabor-based PINNs that rely on multiplicative filters or auxiliary networks to learn Gabor parameters, our approach redefines the network's task as learning a nonlinear mapping from input coordinates to a custom Gabor coordinate system, where a Gabor function captures the dominant oscillatory behavior of the wavefield. This formulation absorbs the effect of two Gabor parameters into the learned mapping, reducing computational complexity and eliminating the need for manual tuning of hyperparameters. We also present an efficient formulation for incorporating a Perfectly Matched Layer (PML) into the training by deriving real-valued loss components and introducing an analytical expression for the background wavefield. Numerical experiments on various velocity models show that our Gabor-PINN achieves faster convergence, higher accuracy, and greater robustness to architectural design and initialization compared to both traditional PINNs and prior Gabor-based methods. The improvement lies not in adding architectural complexity --as is common in enhanced PINNs -- but in absorbing this complexity into the learned coordinate transformation, making the method both simpler and more effective. Our implementation is publicly available to support reproducibility and future research.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Mahdi Abedi, David Pardo, Tariq Alkhalifah

item.title: GVPO: Group Variance Policy Optimization for Large Language Model Post-Training
item.description: arXiv:2504.19599v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Post-training plays a crucial role in refining and aligning large language models to meet specific tasks and human preferences. While recent advancements in post-training techniques, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), leverage increased sampling with relative reward scoring to achieve superior performance, these methods often suffer from training instability that limits their practical adoption. As a next step, we present Group Variance Policy Optimization (GVPO). GVPO incorporates the analytical solution to KL-constrained reward maximization directly into its gradient weights, ensuring alignment with the optimal policy. The method provides intuitive physical interpretations: its gradient mirrors the mean squared error between the central distance of implicit rewards and that of actual rewards. GVPO offers two key advantages: (1) it guarantees a unique optimal solution, exactly the KL-constrained reward maximization objective, (2) it supports flexible sampling distributions that avoids on-policy and importance sampling limitations. By unifying theoretical guarantees with practical adaptability, GVPO establishes a new paradigm for reliable and versatile LLM post-training.
item.dc:creator: Kaichen Zhang, Yuzhong Hong, Junwei Bao, Hongfei Jiang, Yang Song, Dingqian Hong, Hui Xiong

item.title: GARG-AML against Smurfing: A Scalable and Interpretable Graph-Based Framework for Anti-Money Laundering
item.description: arXiv:2506.04292v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Money laundering, a global problem estimated to account for 2%-5% of the global GDP, required regulators to enforce stringent rules on financial institutions to combat it. One prominent laundering method, called smurfing, relies on breaking up transactions into smaller amounts to evade detection. Given the complexity of laundering schemes, involving numerous transactions across multiple parties, network analytics is an important tool for anti-money laundering. However, recent advances in network analytics have leaned heavily on black-box network embedding methods, limiting their utility in businesses. To address the specific nature of smurfing and banks' operational requirements, this paper introduces GARG-AML, a novel graph-based method that quantifies smurfing risk through a single interpretable metric derived from the structure of the second-order transaction network. Unlike traditional methods, GARG-AML provides a balance between computational efficiency and transparency, enabling integration into existing AML workflows. We demonstrate the scalability of GARG-AML on large random networks, and its performance on two open-source money laundering datasets. Our results highlight the potential of GARG-AML to enhance smurfing detection and support investigative decision-making.
item.dc:creator: Bruno Deprez, Bart Baesens, Tim Verdonck, Wouter Verbeke

item.title: Optimal estimates for the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants of deep random ReLU neural networks
item.description: arXiv:2506.19695v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper studies the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants of ReLU neural networks $\Phi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ with random parameters for $p \in [1,\infty]$. The distribution of the weights follows a variant of the He initialization. In the case of zero-bias networks, we derive matching high-probability upper and lower bounds for wide networks that differ at most by an absolute constant. The bounds reveal two remarkable phenomena. First, the bounds grow root-logarithmically in terms of the depth of the net. Second, the behavior of the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants varies significantly between the regimes $p \in [1,2)$ and $p \in [2,\infty]$. For $p \in [2,\infty]$, the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constant behaves similarly to $\|g\|_{p'}$, where $g \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a standard Gaussian vector and $1/p + 1/p' = 1$. In contrast, for $p \in [1,2)$, the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constant aligns more closely with $\|g\|_2$. For networks with possibly nonzero biases, we obtain the same lower bounds without assumptions on the bias distributions. For symmetric bias distributions with bounded densities, we also derive high-probability upper bounds for the $\ell^p$-Lipschitz constants. For fixed sub-exponential bias distributions, these upper bounds differ from the lower bounds by a factor that has square-root dependence on the depth and logarithmic dependence on the width.
item.dc:creator: Sjoerd Dirksen, Patrick Finke, Paul Geuchen, Dominik St\"oger, Felix Voigtlaender

item.title: NeuralDMD: Interpretable Neural Representation of Dynamics from Sparse and Noisy Measurements
item.description: arXiv:2507.03094v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many challenges in scientific imaging involve solving ill-posed inverse problems, where the goal is to recover spatio-temporal fields from indirect, noisy, and highly sparse measurements - often without access to ground truth data or reliable simulators. To address this challenging scenario, we present NeuralDMD, an interpretable, untrained (per-instance) reconstruction framework that combines neural implicit representations with Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to reconstruct continuous spatio-temporal dynamics directly from measurements. NeuralDMD parameterizes DMD modes as continuous neural fields, and imposes a low-rank linear dynamics prior with spectral time evolution to enforce temporal continuity. This formulation enables both forecasting under sparsity, and yields interpretable modes and spectra. We find that NeuralDMD outperforms baselines on a wide variety of tasks: from weather data assimilation from sparse station observations to interferometric (Fourier domain) observations of Sagittarius A, the black hole at the center of our galaxy. Moreover, NeuralDMD remains stable when extrapolating into the future. While this framework is most naturally suited to linear dynamics, we show that it can be applied to nonlinear regimes, though with extrapolation performance that degrades with increasing nonlinearity. Together, these results show that NeuralDMD enables interpretable reconstruction and forecasting of spatio-temporal dynamics directly from sparse and indirect measurements without relying on numerical simulators or training data.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Computer Vision - ECCV 2026, Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 17038, pp. 1-20 (2026)
item.dc:creator: Ali SaraerToosi, Renbo Tu, Esther Y. H. Lin, Kamyar Azizzadenesheli, Aviad Levis

item.title: A Survey of Explainable Reinforcement Learning: Targets, Methods and Needs
item.description: arXiv:2507.12599v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The success of recent Artificial Intelligence (AI) models has been accompanied by the opacity of their internal mechanisms, due notably to the use of deep neural networks. In order to understand these internal mechanisms and explain the output of these AI models, a set of methods have been proposed, grouped under the domain of eXplainable AI (XAI). This paper focuses on a sub-domain of XAI, called eXplainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL), which aims to explain the actions of an agent that has learned by reinforcement learning. We propose an intuitive taxonomy based on two questions "What" and "How". The first question focuses on the target that the method explains, while the second relates to the way the explanation is provided. We use this taxonomy to provide a state-of-the-art review of over 250 papers. In addition, we present a set of domains close to XRL, which we believe should get attention from the community. Finally, we identify some needs for the field of XRL.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research 87, Article 16 (October 2026)
item.dc:creator: L\'eo Sauli\`eres

item.title: Missing value imputation with adversarial random forests - MissARF
item.description: arXiv:2507.15681v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Handling missing values is a common challenge in biostatistical analyses, typically addressed by imputation methods. We propose a novel, fast, and easy-to-use imputation method called missing value imputation with adversarial random forests (MissARF), based on generative machine learning, that provides both single and multiple imputation. MissARF employs adversarial random forest (ARF) for density estimation and data synthesis. To impute a missing value of an observation, we condition on the non-missing values and sample from the estimated conditional distribution generated by ARF. Our experiments demonstrate that MissARF performs comparably to state-of-the-art single and multiple imputation methods in terms of imputation quality and fast runtime with no additional costs for multiple imputation.
item.dc:creator: Pegah Golchian, Jan Kapar, David S. Watson, Marvin N. Wright

item.title: Confidence Calibration in Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2507.17383v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Trustworthy robot behavior requires not only high levels of task success but also that the robot can reliably quantify how likely it is to succeed. To this end, we present a first-of-its-kind study of confidence calibration in vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models, which map visual observations and natural language instructions to low-level robot motor commands. We establish a confidence estimation baseline for VLAs, examine how task success relates to calibration error and how calibration evolves over time, and introduce two lightweight techniques to remedy the miscalibration we observe: prompt ensembles and action-wise Platt scaling. Our aim in this study is to begin to develop the tools and conceptual understanding necessary to render VLAs trustworthy via reliable uncertainty quantification.
item.dc:creator: Thomas P Zollo, Richard Zemel

item.title: Reinforcement Learning in MDPs with Information-Ordered Policies
item.description: arXiv:2508.03904v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Many operational Markov decision processes provide structured information where a trajectory generated under one policy may also reveal how other policies would have performed. We formalize this through an information order over a parameterized policy class, writing $\pi_{\theta'} \preceq \pi_\theta$ when data collected under $\pi_\theta$ can be used to estimate the long-run average cost of $\pi_{\theta'}$. We develop an epoch-based reinforcement learning algorithm for infinite-horizon average-cost MDPs with continuous state and action spaces that exploits this order through counterfactual inference. For a $d$-dimensional policy class whose information order has width $w$, the algorithm achieves $\widetilde O(H\sqrt{wdT/\alpha})$ regret relative to the optimal policy in the class, where $H$ is a bias span upper bound and $\alpha$ denotes an "information ratio". Thus, the width captures the effective exploration complexity of the problem, interpolating between full counterfactual feedback and unstructured policy learning. We instantiate the framework in lost-sales inventory systems with positive lead times, dual-sourcing systems governed by dual-index policies, and queues with state-dependent service rates. These applications yield new regret guarantees without requiring global convexity of the average-cost function or specialized arrival-rate structure. Numerical experiments show that exploiting the information order substantially improves learning performance over existing general-purpose and problem-specific benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Zhongjun Zhang, Shipra Agrawal, Ilan Lobel, Sean R. Sinclair, Christina Lee Yu

item.title: The Statistical Fairness-Accuracy Frontier
item.description: arXiv:2508.17622v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study fairness-accuracy tradeoffs when a single predictive model must serve multiple demographic groups. A useful tool for understanding this tradeoff is the fairness-accuracy (FA) Pareto frontier, which characterizes the set of models that cannot be improved in either fairness or accuracy without worsening the other. While characterizing the FA frontier requires full knowledge of the data distribution, we focus on the finite-sample regime, quantifying how well a designer can approximate any point on the frontier from limited data and bounding the worst-case gap. In particular, we derive worst-case-optimal estimators that depend on the designer's knowledge of the covariate distribution. For each estimator, we characterize how finite-sample effects asymmetrically impact each group's welfare and identify optimal sample allocation strategies. Finally, we provide uniform finite-sample bounds along the entire FA frontier, quantifying finite-sample deviations across alternative fairness-accuracy tradeoffs.
item.dc:creator: Alireza Fallah, Michael I. Jordan, Annie Ulichney

item.title: Practical and Private Hybrid ML Inference with Fully Homomorphic Encryption
item.description: arXiv:2509.01253v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In contemporary cloud-based services, protecting users' sensitive data and ensuring the confidentiality of the server's model are critical. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables inference directly on encrypted inputs, but its practicality is hindered by expensive bootstrapping and inefficient approximations of non-linear activations. We introduce Safhire, a hybrid inference framework that executes linear layers under encryption on the server while offloading non- linearities to the client in plaintext. This design eliminates bootstrapping, supports exact activations, and significantly reduces computation cost. To safeguard model confidentiality despite client access to intermediate outputs, Safhire applies randomized shuffling, which obfuscates intermediate values and makes it practically impossible for a client to reconstruct the model. To further reduce inference latency, Safhire incorporates advanced optimizations such as fast ciphertext packing and partial extraction. Evaluations on multiple standard models and datasets show that Safhire achieves up to 7.6x and 7.4x lower inference latency than Orion and Concrete-ML, respectively, which are two state-of-the-art FHE baselines, with manageable communication overhead and comparable accuracy. These results underline the practicality of our hybrid FHE inference scheme.
item.dc:creator: Sayan Biswas, Philippe Chartier, Akash Dhasade, Tom Jurien, David Kerriou, Anne-Marie Kerrmarec, Mohammed Lemou, Franklin Tranie, Martijn de Vos, Milos Vujasinovic

item.title: Board gender diversity and emissions performance: Insights from panel regressions, machine learning, and explainable AI
item.description: arXiv:2510.00244v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: With European Union initiatives mandating gender quotas on corporate boards, a key question arises: Is greater board gender diversity (BGD) associated with better emissions performance (EP)? To answer this question, we examine the influence of BGD on EP across a sample of European firms from 2016 to 2022. Using panel regressions, advanced machine learning algorithms, and explainable AI, we reveal a non-linear relationship. Specifically, EP improves with BGD up to an optimal level of approximately 35 %, beyond which further increases in BGD yield no additional improvement in EP. A minimum BGD threshold of 22 % is necessary for meaningful improvements in EP. To assess the legitimacy of EP outcomes, this study examines whether ESG controversies weaken the BGD-EP relationship. The results show no significant effect, suggesting that BGD's impact is driven by governance mechanisms rather than symbolic actions. Additionally, path analysis indicates that while environmental innovation contributes to EP, it is not the mediating channel through which BGD promotes EP. The results have implications for academics, businesses, and regulators.
item.dc:creator: Mohammad Hassan Shakil, Arne Johan Pollestad, Khine Kyaw, Ziaul Haque Munim

item.title: Language steering in latent space to mitigate unintended code-switching
item.description: arXiv:2510.13849v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multilingual Large Language Models (LLMs) often exhibit hallucinations such as unintended code-switching, reducing reliability in downstream tasks. We propose latent-space language steering, a lightweight inference-time method that identifies language directions via Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on parallel translations and steers token embeddings along these axes to control language identity. Our approach mitigates code-switching (reduced next-token distributional divergence by up to 55\%, reduced Code-Switching Index by 63--99\%) while preserving broad semantic direction with negligible computational overhead and requires only minimal parallel data for calibration. Additionally, we evaluate language classification using a single principal component (95-99\% accuracy) and further analyze the layer-wise evolution of language representations.
item.dc:creator: Andrey Goncharov, Nikolai Kondusov, Alexey Zaytsev

item.title: Reliable data clustering with Bayesian community detection
item.description: arXiv:2510.15013v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: From neuroscience and genomics to systems biology and ecology, researchers rely on clustering similarity data to uncover modular structure. Most methods work in two steps: first reduce noise, then cluster. The first step runs without regard to the second: it forces arbitrary choices, discards useful information, and can impose structure where none exists. Here we bring the two steps together. Using established Bayesian community detection methods, we let one minimum description length criterion choose both how much to sparsify the data and how to cluster it. This one-step approach keeps all the samples for inference, removes the arbitrary threshold choice, and returns a single cluster when there is no real structure. On synthetic data, our approach recovers clusters under more noise and with fewer samples than standard methods. On gene co-expression data from the human brain, it finds more coherent and more stable clusters than WGCNA, the standard tool in the field. Uniting sparsification and clustering in a single model-selection step provides a principled, noise-resistant way to uncover modular structure in similarity data across fields.
item.dc:creator: Magnus Neuman, Jelena Smiljani\'c, Martin Rosvall

item.title: Rep2Text: Decoding Full Text from a Single LLM Token Representation
item.description: arXiv:2511.06571v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models represent text as hidden numerical patterns, but what information these representations actually contain remains a mystery. Can we recover the original text from just one of them? In this paper, we introduce Rep2Text, a method designed to answer this question by reconstructing text from a single hidden representation. We find that these representations preserve much more information than we might expect. For short texts of about 16 words, Rep2Text can recover roughly half of the original words while preserving their overall meaning. As the text gets longer, recovering the exact wording becomes harder, but the main ideas can still be recovered. These findings offer a new way to understand what language models store internally and highlight potential privacy risks, as hidden representations may reveal parts of the original input.
item.dc:creator: Haiyan Zhao, Zirui He, Yiming Tang, Fan Yang, Ali Payani, Dianbo Liu, Mengnan Du

item.title: Robust Experimental Design via Generalised Bayesian Inference
item.description: arXiv:2511.07671v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bayesian optimal experimental design is a principled framework for conducting experiments that leverages Bayesian inference to quantify how much information one can expect to gain from selecting a certain design. However, accurate Bayesian inference relies on the assumption that one's statistical model of the data-generating process is correctly specified. If this assumption is violated, Bayesian methods can lead to poor inference and estimates of information gain. Generalised Bayesian (or Gibbs) inference is a more robust probabilistic inference framework that replaces the likelihood in the Bayesian update by a suitable loss function. In this work, we present Generalised Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design (GBOED), an extension of generalised Bayesian inference to the experimental design setting which achieves robustness in both design and inference. Using a generalisation of Bayesian decision theory, we derive a new acquisition function, the Gibbs expected information gain. Our empirical results demonstrate that GBOED can enhance robustness to outliers and incorrect assumptions about the outcome noise distribution.
item.dc:creator: Yasir Zubayr Barlas, Sabina J. Sloman, Samuel Kaski

item.title: Operon: Incremental Construction of Ragged Data via Named Dimensions
item.description: arXiv:2511.16080v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern data processing workflows frequently encounter ragged data: collections with variable-length elements that arise naturally in domains like natural language processing, scientific measurements, and autonomous AI agents. Existing workflow engines lack native support for tracking the shapes and dependencies inherent to ragged data, forcing users to manage complex indexing and dependency bookkeeping manually. We present Operon, a Rust-based workflow engine that addresses these challenges through a novel formalism of named dimensions with explicit dependency relations. Operon provides a domain-specific language where users declare pipelines with dimension annotations that are statically verified for correctness, while the runtime system dynamically schedules tasks as data shapes are incrementally discovered during execution. We formalize the mathematical foundation for reasoning about partial shapes and prove that Operon's incremental construction algorithm guarantees deterministic and confluent execution in parallel settings. The system's explicit modeling of partially-known states enables robust persistence and recovery mechanisms, while its per-task multi-queue architecture achieves efficient parallelism across heterogeneous task types. Empirical evaluation demonstrates that Operon outperforms an existing workflow engine with 14.94x baseline overhead reduction while maintaining near-linear end-to-end output rates as workloads scale, making it particularly suitable for large-scale data generation pipelines in machine learning applications.
item.dc:creator: Sungbin Moon, Jiho Park, Suyoung Hwang, Donghyun Koh, Seunghyun Moon, Minhyeong Lee

item.title: CoatFusion: Controllable Material Coating in Images
item.description: arXiv:2512.02143v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce Material Coating, a novel image editing task that simulates applying a thin material layer onto an object while preserving its underlying coarse and fine geometry. Material coating is fundamentally different from existing "material transfer" methods, which are designed to replace an object's intrinsic material, often overwriting fine details. To address this new task, we construct a large-scale synthetic dataset (110K images) of 3D objects with varied, physically-based coatings, named DataCoat110K. We then propose CoatFusion, a novel architecture that enables this task by conditioning a diffusion model on both a 2D albedo texture and granular, PBR-style parametric controls, including roughness, metalness, transmission, and a key thickness parameter. Experiments and user studies show CoatFusion produces realistic, controllable coatings and significantly outperforms existing material editing and transfer methods on this new task.
item.dc:creator: Sagie Levy, Elad Aharoni, Matan Levy, Ariel Shamir, Dani Lischinski

item.title: AceFF: A State-of-the-Art Machine Learning Potential for Small Molecules
item.description: arXiv:2601.00581v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce AceFF, a pre-trained machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) optimized for small molecule drug discovery. While MLIPs have emerged as efficient alternatives to Density Functional Theory (DFT), generalizability across diverse chemical spaces remains difficult. AceFF addresses this by refining the TensorNet2 architecture and training it on a comprehensive dataset of drug-like compounds. This approach yields a force field that balances high-throughput inference speed with DFT-level accuracy. We introduce two models sharing the same architecture: \mbox{AceFF-2}, trained on our own dataset of small molecules and supporting the essential medicinal chemistry elements (H, B, C, N, O, F, Si, P, S, Cl, Br, I); and \mbox{AceFF-2-OMOL}, trained on a subset of OMol25 containing the AceFF-2 elements plus the common biomolecular ion elements Na and K. The models are explicitly trained to handle charged states. Validation against rigorous benchmarks, including complex torsional energy scans, molecular dynamics trajectories, batched minimizations, and tests of force and energy accuracy, demonstrates that AceFF is state-of-the-art for organic molecules in the accuracy and speed regime important for drug discovery. The AceFF-2 and AceFF-2-OMol model weights and inference code are available at https://huggingface.co/Acellera/AceFF-2.0 and https://huggingface.co/Acellera/AceFF-2-OMOL.
item.dc:creator: Stephen E. Farr, Stefan Doerr, Antonio Mirarchi, Alireza Moradzadeh, Francesc Sabanes Zariquiey, Saee Paliwal, Gianni De Fabritiis

item.title: Pro-AI Bias in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2601.13749v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for decision-support across multiple domains. We ask whether these models favor artificial intelligence (AI) itself. We examine this question through three experiments. First, in open-ended advice across investment, study, career, and startup domains, AI is prominent in most recommendation lists and is usually ranked first when it appears. Second, in salary estimations, models overestimate AI-related jobs more than they do for closely matched non-AI jobs. In a controlled follow-up, changing only the job title from the matched non-AI title to the AI-related title raises predicted salary by 10%, while all other supplied job details remain fixed. Finally, we show that the number of degrees and other credentials awarded by AI programs were 28% more overestimated than corresponding awards for matched computing programs. Overall, we show that AI is not only prominent in everyday LLM advice, but also receives systematically inflated quantitative estimates compared to non-AI cases, even against its closest disciplinary neighbors, raising concerns for high-stakes decision support.
item.dc:creator: Benaya Trabelsi, Jonathan Shaki, Sarit Kraus

item.title: AutoPrunedRetriever: Persistent Reasoning Graphs for Efficient and Extensible Retrieval-Augmented Generation
item.description: arXiv:2602.04926v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become a standard approach for knowledge-intensive LLM tasks. Complex reasoning remains challenging because queries often require composing dispersed evidence through multiple dependent reasoning steps. Yet existing RAG systems process queries independently, repeatedly retrieving overlapping evidence and reconstructing established reasoning. Preserving such reasoning makes previously retrieved evidence and intermediate results reusable for subsequent queries. However, inference-time reuse becomes increasingly costly as the history grows, motivating a compact representation that preserves useful information without substantial loss in quality. To address these challenges, we present AutoPrunedRetriever (APR), a graph-based RAG system that encodes corpus facts and query-derived reasoning in a shared symbolic codebook. The codebook serves both as the retrieval index and as persistent memory, representing facts, questions, and answers as compact edge sequences, so that the previously established structure can be directly retrieved and reused. At inference time, APR retrieves query-specific reasoning paths and constructs compact prompts, while incremental consolidation keeps the growing memory compact. For deployments where the retriever cannot be replaced, we introduce AutoPruned Layer (APL), which leaves host retrieval unchanged but replaces the retrieved context with the corresponding entries in the shared symbolic codebook, writing each question and answer back as a compact structure. Across five complex-reasoning benchmarks, APR improves accuracy over the strongest baseline by 1.8-10.8 points while using up to 96% fewer input tokens. APL reduces generator input by 60-96% across host systems and preserves answer quality on document-style contexts.
item.dc:creator: Ning Wang, Kuanyan Zhu, Daniel Yuehwoon Yee, Yitang Gao, Shiying Huang, Zirun Xu, Sainyam Galhotra

item.title: A Theoretical Analysis of Test-Driven Code Generation
item.description: arXiv:2602.06098v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Code assistants are increasingly utilized in test-driven software development, yet the theoretical mechanisms behind their environment-interaction strategies remain underexplored. We provide a probabilistic framework for two dominant paradigms: code selection after generation using the execution environment, and code generation conditioned on environment feedback. First, we formalize several well-established selection heuristics as environment-aware estimators of code correctness. We theoretically prove that estimators based on fuzzy functional similarity add an inductive bias and strictly dominate estimators based on functional equivalence in terms of signal-to-noise ratio. Second, we frame backprompting as an in-context approximation of Thompson sampling. We derive a novel regret bound for reward functions with unobservable components, theoretically explaining why the effectiveness of backprompting is limited by the ambiguity of the informal task description (an irreducible regret). Using seven state-of-the-art open weight models, we corroborate these findings across BigCodeBenchHard, LeetCodeDataset, QiskitHumanEvalSim, and SWE-bench Verified. Our formalization also suggests how to improve task descriptions effectively, leading to an improved benchmark for LLM-assisted quantum programming, QiskitHumanEvalSimX.
item.dc:creator: Nicolas Menet, Michael Hersche, Andreas Krause, Abbas Rahimi

item.title: Structural Causal Bottleneck Models
item.description: arXiv:2603.08682v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce structural causal bottleneck models (SCBMs), a novel class of structural causal models in which causal effects between high-dimensional variables are mediated by low-dimensional summary statistics, or *bottlenecks*. SCBMs provide a flexible framework for mechanism-specific, target-dependent dimension reduction while remaining estimable via standard learning algorithms. We prove that bottleneck variables are identifiable up to bijection from observational data, and validate this experimentally. We then study causal effect estimation in linear SCBMs under three standard adjustment strategies. For instrumental variables, we identify a population-level non-identifiability of na\"ive two-stage least squares when all variables are high-dimensional, and show that bottleneck representations restore identification. For mediation and backdoor adjustment, we prove that conditioning on bottleneck variables yields valid effect estimates with explicit finite-sample efficiency gains over conditioning on full high-dimensional variables. We argue that SCBMs provide a principled alternative to existing causal dimension reduction frameworks such as causal representation learning and causal abstractions.
item.dc:creator: Simon Bing, Jonas Wahl, Jakob Runge

item.title: Detecting Multi-Agent Collusion Through Multi-Agent Interpretability
